summary: Defines a MIB module for managing virtual machines controlled by a hypervisor, also known as a virtual machine monitor, with objects to describe and manage them.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a list of dials for watching pretend computers that live inside a real one.

questions: how to manage virtual machines with snmp
how to monitor virtual machines with snmp
subtitle: A standard set of SNMP objects for watching the virtual machines a hypervisor runs and the resources it gives them.

tldr.problem: Hypervisors such as Xen and VMware each had their own product-specific MIB modules, so there was no common way to manage virtual machines over SNMP.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7666 defines VM-MIB, a MIB module with scalars about the hypervisor and tables for virtual machines, virtual CPUs, storage devices and network interfaces, plus notifications when a machine changes state.
tldr.outcome: Operators get one general set of objects, kept at the hypervisor, that describes what each virtual machine has been allocated rather than what its guest operating system actually uses.

today: RFC 7666 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2015, and the unit data shows nothing that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Virtual Machine MIB
sections.content:
A hypervisor (also called a virtual machine monitor) controls several virtual machines on one physical machine by giving each of them a share of the physical resources. RFC 7666 defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for the information a hypervisor holds about those virtual machines and about its own hardware and software.

The design is derived from product-specific MIB modules: one for guests of the Xen hypervisor, one for virtual machines controlled by the VMware hypervisor, and one built on the libvirt programming interface. This RFC tries to generalize those objects so that other hypervisor implementations can support them too.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a building manager who hands out rooms to tenants. This document is the standard clipboard the manager uses to note who lives where and what they were given.

sections.title: Overview and Objectives
sections.content:
The module covers system and software information about the hypervisor, the list of virtual machines it controls, and the virtual resources allocated to them. It specifies four kinds of virtual resource common to many hypervisors: processors (CPUs), memory, network interfaces (NICs) and storage devices. The objects do not depend on which family of hypervisor or which operating system runs inside the virtual machines.

The objects live at the hypervisor, because the hypervisor manages the virtual resources. When SNMP is used, an SNMP agent runs at the hypervisor to give access to them.

The viewpoint is that of the hypervisor operator, not the operator of a virtual machine. The objects describe resource allocation, not actual utilization. For example, vmStorageAllocatedSize is the size allocated by the hypervisor, not the size the guest operating system actually uses. For the vmNetworkIfIndex interface, 'in' means from a virtual machine to the hypervisor and 'out' means from the hypervisor to a virtual machine.
sections.plainLanguage: The manager only writes down which rooms were handed out, not how messy each tenant keeps theirs.

sections.title: Structure of the VM-MIB Module
sections.content:
The module is a group of scalars and tables. The scalars below vmHypervisor give basic facts about the hypervisor, such as vmHvSoftware, vmHvVersion, vmHvObjectID and vmHvUpTime.

  • vmTable lists the virtual machines (guests) known to the hypervisor.
  • vmCpuTable maps virtual CPUs to virtual machines and includes the CPU time each virtual CPU has used.
  • vmCpuAffinityTable gives the affinity of each virtual CPU to a physical CPU.
  • vmStorageTable lists virtual storage devices and maps them to virtual machines. An entry can point to its physical parent through vmStorageParent.
  • vmNetworkTable lists virtual network interfaces and maps them to virtual machines. Each entry points to an entry in the ifTable of the IF-MIB through vmNetworkIfIndex, and can point to a physical parent through vmNetworkParent.

The module is registered as { mib-2 236 }.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one sheet for the tenants, one for the brains they were given, one for their storage closets and one for their phone lines. Each sheet points back to the right tenant.

sections.title: Machine States and Notifications
sections.content:
Two textual conventions model the life of a virtual machine. vmAdminState is the state an administrator asks for: running(1), suspended(2), paused(3) or shutdown(4). vmOperState is the state the machine is actually in, with values such as preparing(3), running(4), suspending(5), suspended(6), resuming(7), paused(8), migrating(9), shuttingdown(10), shutdown(11) and crashed(12). Suspending, resuming and shutting down are transient states.

Events that move a machine between major operational states cause notifications. Per-VM notifications (for example vmRunning and vmCrashed) are sent when vmPerVMNotificationsEnabled is true(1). Bulk notifications (for example vmBulkRunning) are sent when vmBulkNotificationsEnabled is true(1).

Bulk notifications exist to cut the number of notifications an SNMP manager receives. The RFC notes that a data center could have several thousand virtual machines, and per-VM notifications carry more detail but do not scale well. Managers control notifications with the filtering mechanism of RFC 3413.
sections.plainLanguage: Each tenant has a status light: running, sleeping, moving out and so on. A bell rings when a light changes. If hundreds change at once, one big bell can ring for the whole group instead.

sections.title: Relationship to Other MIB Modules
sections.content:
VM-MIB is built to work with existing MIBs. On systems that implement the HOST-RESOURCES-MIB (RFC 2790), vmCpuPhysIndex points to a processor in the hrProcessorTable and vmStorageParent points to a storage device in the hrStorageTable.

The IF-MIB (RFC 2863) must contain both physical and virtual network interfaces in its ifTable, and vmNetworkTable points into it.

Virtual switch objects are left out because virtual network interfaces are the lowest abstraction of network resources given to a virtual machine; the IEEE8021-BRIDGE-MIB and IEEE8021-Q-BRIDGE-MIB could be used instead. Hypervisor-specific items such as management IP addresses of a virtual machine are also left out, and may be placed in the entLogicalTable of the ENTITY-MIB. The new vmHvUpTime and vmHvObjectID complement sysUpTime, sysObjectID and hrSystemUptime.
sections.plainLanguage: The new clipboard does not repeat what other clipboards already record. It just points to them.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC defines the first version of the IANA-maintained IANA-STORAGE-MEDIA-TYPE-MIB module, which lets new storage media types be added to the IANAStorageMediaType enumeration. An Expert Review is REQUIRED for each modification.

Two object identifiers are recorded in the SMI Numbers registry: vmMIB as { mib-2 236 } and ianaStorageMediaTypeMIB as { mib-2 237 }.
sections.plainLanguage: A keeper of the official list of storage types adds new kinds when an expert agrees they are real.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module is typically implemented on the hypervisor, not inside a virtual machine. Virtual machines, possibly under other administrative domains, would not normally reach it because the SNMP service usually runs on a separate management network.

Two objects are read-write: vmPerVMNotificationsEnabled and vmBulkNotificationsEnabled. Turning notifications on could produce a substantial number of them if many machines change state at once. The RFC RECOMMENDS making them read-only where SNMPv3 strong security (authentication and encryption) is not used.

Other objects may be sensitive too. Software and version objects could help an attacker, and the VM and resource tables reveal how many and which virtual machines an operator runs. Even GET access should be controlled. SNMPv1 is not secure, and the RFC recommends the SNMPv3 User-based Security Model and View-based Access Control Model.
sections.plainLanguage: The tenant list is private. Only the right people should be allowed to look at it or change the bell settings.
